examTakeaway: Bite cells after an oxidant drug mean NADPH could not be refilled, so hemoglobin denatured into Heinz bodies.
scenario: A 20-year-old man develops dark urine two days after primaquine. Hemoglobin is 9 g/dL. The smear shows bite cells. A special stain shows clumps of denatured hemoglobin. Coombs test is negative. He is of Mediterranean ancestry. He asks which cofactor his red cells could not regenerate.
question: Which cofactor could the red cells not refill?
explanation: Bite cells after an oxidant drug mean NADPH could not be refilled, so hemoglobin denatured into Heinz bodies. NADPH is the cofactor glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase supplies, and without it glutathione cannot be restored. ATP from pyruvate kinase is a different hemolysis without oxidant bites. Spectrin loss makes spherocytes, not bites. Heme deficiency is a sideroblastic production problem. Glucose-6-phosphatase product in the liver is von Gierke disease, not an oxidant hemolysis.

examTakeaway: Morning hemoglobinuria plus a venous clot means complement is punching red cells that lost their GPI-anchored shields.
scenario: A 32-year-old man has cola-colored urine on the first morning void that clears later. LDH is high. He has had a mesenteric vein clot. Flow cytometry shows red cells missing two complement-shield proteins. Coombs test is negative. He asks why complement is now able to lyse the cells.
question: Which shield is missing from the red-cell surface?
explanation: Morning hemoglobinuria plus a venous clot means complement is punching red cells that lost their GPI-anchored shields. GPI-anchored CD55 and CD59 are those shields, and their loss also lets platelets form clot. Spectrin loss is spherocytosis without this morning hemoglobinuria and unusual thrombosis. A hemoglobin beta chain defect is thalassemia or sickle cell disease. von Willebrand factor deficiency causes bleeding. ADAMTS13 deficiency is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, led by schistocytes and low platelets.

examTakeaway: A very low MCV with a normal ferritin and a raised HbA2 means beta chains are underproduced, so delta chains rise.
scenario: A 24-year-old man has a hemoglobin of 11 g/dL and an MCV of 68 fL. Ferritin is normal. The smear shows target cells. HbA2 is 6 percent. There are no ring sideroblasts. He asks why a minor hemoglobin fraction rose.
question: Which globin shortfall raises HbA2?
explanation: A very low MCV with a normal ferritin and a raised HbA2 means beta chains are underproduced, so delta chains rise. Beta globin is the shortfall, and HbA2 is alpha2-delta2. Four alpha genes deleted is fatal hydrops, not a walking adult. A heme enzyme defect makes ring sideroblasts. Spectrin loss makes spherocytes. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is episodic oxidant hemolysis, not a high HbA2.

examTakeaway: A very high granulocyte count with a low alkaline-phosphatase score is a BCR-ABL clone, not a reactive marrow.
scenario: A 55-year-old man has a white count of 120,000/mm3 with myelocytes and few blasts. The leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score is low. He has no fever and no abscess. The spleen is large. Cytogenetics are pending. He asks why this does not look like a reaction to infection.
question: Which fusion keeps this count from being a reaction?
options: A leukemoid reaction, which would raise the score
explanation: A very high granulocyte count with a low alkaline-phosphatase score is a BCR-ABL clone, not a reactive marrow. BCR-ABL drives the granulocytes and the enzyme score stays low. A leukemoid reaction, which would raise the score, needs a fever or an abscess he does not have. PML-RARA is acute promyelocytic leukemia with bleeding. c-MYC of Burkitt lymphoma is a B-cell tumor, not this white count. BCL2 of follicular lymphoma is a slow node disease.

examTakeaway: TdT-positive, peroxidase-negative blasts in a child are lymphoid, because TdT is the lymphoid marker and Auer rods are absent.
scenario: A 6-year-old boy has bone pain and pallor. Blasts fill the marrow. They mark with TdT and the peroxidase stain is negative. No Auer rods are seen. There is no mediastinal mass. He asks which lineage the negative peroxidase supports.
question: Which lineage fits a positive TdT and a negative peroxidase?
explanation: TdT-positive, peroxidase-negative blasts in a child are lymphoid, because TdT is the lymphoid marker and Auer rods are absent. Lymphoid blasts fit that pair of stains. Myeloid blasts are often peroxidase positive and may show Auer rods. Promyelocytic blasts are a myeloid subset with granules. Megakaryocytic blasts mark for platelets. Erythroid blasts are not TdT positive.

examTakeaway: A jaw mass of medium lymphocytes with pale macrophages means c-MYC was placed next to the immunoglobulin promoter.
scenario: An 8-year-old boy has a rapidly growing jaw mass. Biopsy shows medium lymphocytes and scattered pale macrophages. A translocation joins chromosome 8 to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus on 14. There is no Philadelphia chromosome. He asks which gene on 8 was moved.
question: Which gene was placed next to the immunoglobulin promoter?
explanation: A jaw mass of medium lymphocytes with pale macrophages means c-MYC was placed next to the immunoglobulin promoter. c-MYC is the chromosome 8 gene in that translocation. BCR-ABL is the 9;22 fusion. BCL2 is t(14;18) of follicular lymphoma. Cyclin D1 is t(11;14) of mantle cell lymphoma. PML-RARA is t(15;17) of acute promyelocytic leukemia.

examTakeaway: Punched-out bone and light chains in the urine mean a plasma-cell clone is injuring bone and the kidney, not a node-based lymphoma.
scenario: A 68-year-old man has back pain and a creatinine of 2.2 mg/dL. The skull film shows round holes. Red cells stack on the smear. Urine has light chains and little albumin. Calcium is 11.4 mg/dL. A node is not the enlarged tissue. He asks which cell is making the light chains.
question: Which cell is secreting the light chains that injure the kidney?
options: A mature small lymphocyte of CLL
explanation: Punched-out bone and light chains in the urine mean a plasma-cell clone is injuring bone and the kidney, not a node-based lymphoma. Plasma cell clones secrete the light chains and punch bone. Reed-Sternberg cell is Hodgkin lymphoma in a node. Myeloblast is acute myeloid leukemia. Lymphoblast is childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia. A mature small lymphocyte of CLL raises the lymphocyte count and makes smudge cells, not skull holes.

examTakeaway: A second clot with a clotting time that activated protein C cannot lengthen is factor V that the protein cannot cut.
scenario: A 28-year-old woman has a second deep-vein thrombosis after a short flight. She is not pregnant and has no cancer. Adding activated protein C does not prolong her clotting time. The prothrombin gene test is negative and an antiphospholipid antibody is negative. She asks which factor resists being cut.
question: Which factor resists activated protein C?
explanation: A second clot with a clotting time that activated protein C cannot lengthen is factor V that the protein cannot cut. Factor V with the Leiden change is not cleaved, so the clotting time stays short. Factor VIII excess can promote clot but is not this resistance assay. Antithrombin deficiency is a different test. Protein C itself being low is a different disease. von Willebrand factor deficiency causes bleeding, not thrombosis.

examTakeaway: Skin necrosis a few days after warfarin happens because protein C falls before the longer-lived clotting factors.
scenario: A 40-year-old woman starts warfarin for a new clot and is not bridged with heparin. On day 3 she has painful black skin on the breasts. Platelets have not fallen. She is not on heparin. A protein measured before any drug was already low, and that protein has a short half-life. She asks why the skin clotted while other factors were still present.
question: Which short-lived anticoagulant fell first?
explanation: Skin necrosis a few days after warfarin happens because protein C falls before the longer-lived clotting factors. Protein C has the short half-life, so an already low level lets clot form in skin. Platelets from heparin antibodies is HIT, and she is not on heparin. ADAMTS13 deficiency is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Factor VIII deficiency bleeds into joints. Fibrinogen in DIC falls with oozing and a low platelet count, not isolated skin necrosis on day 3.

examTakeaway: Clot and miscarriage with a PTT that does not correct on mixing is an antiphospholipid antibody.
scenario: A 29-year-old woman has had three miscarriages after 10 weeks and a prior leg clot. The PTT is prolonged and does not correct when her plasma is mixed with normal plasma. The confirmatory clotting test shortens when extra phospholipid is added. She has no joint bleeding and factor VIII activity is not low.
question: Which inhibitor is present?
explanation: Clot and miscarriage with a PTT that does not correct on mixing is an antiphospholipid antibody. Antiphospholipid antibody prolongs the PTT in the tube but causes thrombosis in the body, and extra phospholipid corrects the assay. A factor VIII antibody also fails to correct on mixing but causes bleeding, and her factor VIII is not low. Heparin in the sample prolongs the PTT but does not explain recurrent miscarriage. Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT more than this story and corrects with mixing if it is a factor deficiency. Hemophilia A is an X-linked factor deficiency that corrects on mixing and bleeds into joints.

examTakeaway: Rigid spherocytes with a high MCHC and a negative Coombs test are trapped in the spleen, which is why splenectomy stops the hemolysis.
scenario: A 15-year-old boy has jaundice and a hemoglobin of 10 g/dL. The smear shows spherocytes and the MCHC is high. Osmotic fragility is increased. Coombs test is negative. His father had the same anemia. There are no bite cells. He asks which organ is destroying the rigid cells.
question: Which organ traps these poorly deformable red cells?
options: The liver sinusoids as the only site
Marrow macrophages as the only site
explanation: Rigid spherocytes with a high MCHC and a negative Coombs test are trapped in the spleen, which is why splenectomy stops the hemolysis. The spleen removes spherocytes that cannot deform. The liver sinusoids as the only site and the lung are not the filter for this membrane defect. The kidney filters plasma, not intact red cells. Marrow macrophages as the only site are not the reason splenectomy ends the hemolysis.
